NP, or nondeterministic polynomial time complexity class. The set of decision problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time, even if finding those solutions may be computationally hard. Formally, it is the set of languages decidable by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time. NP contains P and is the core of the P versus NP problem. The distinction between verifiable in polynomial time and solvable in polynomial time remains one of mathematics' greatest unsolved mysteries and has profound implications for cryptography, optimization, and computational theory. NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time. A problem is in NP if a proposed solution, called a certificate or witness, can be verified in polynomial time O of n to the k. According to the verification-based definition, a problem L is in NP if there exists a polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that for each input x: x is in L if and only if there exists a certificate c of length at most p of the length of x, where V of x and c returns yes. The nondeterministic Turing machine definition states that a problem is in NP if a nondeterministic Turing machine can decide it in polynomial time by guessing a certificate and verifying it. An important asymmetry is that NP is about verification, not solution-finding. A problem can be in NP even if no known polynomial-time algorithm finds the solution. Let me give you examples of NP problems. The Travelling Salesman Problem: given cities and distances, is there a tour visiting all cities with total distance less than or equal to k? Verifying a proposed tour takes O of n time. Boolean Satisfiability, or SAT: given a logical formula, is there an assignment of variables making it true? Verifying a proposed assignment takes O of n time. The Clique Problem: does a graph contain a clique, or complete subgraph, of size greater than or equal to k? Verifying a proposed clique takes O of k squared time. Subset Sum: given integers, is there a subset summing to a target value? Verifying a proposed subset takes O of n time. Integer Factorization: given n, is there a factor in a range from a to b? Verifying a proposed factor takes O of log n time. Graph Coloring: can a graph be colored with less than or equal to k colors such that no adjacent vertices share a color? Verifying a coloring takes O of m time, where m is the number of edges. Several important relationships hold between NP and other complexity classes. P is a subset of NP, which is proven. Every problem solvable in polynomial time can also be verified in polynomial time. Simply ignore the certificate and solve it deterministically. NP is a subset of PSPACE, which is proven. NP problems are solvable in polynomial space, though potentially exponential time. Whether P equals NP is open. It is unknown whether P equals NP. Intuitively, finding a solution seems harder than verifying it, but this remains unproven. Whether NP equals PSPACE is also unknown, though this is generally believed to be false. NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP. Every problem in NP reduces to them in polynomial time. Examples include SAT, TSP, Clique, Subset Sum, three-coloring, Hamiltonian cycle, and Knapsack. The significance is this: if any NP-complete problem is in P, then P equals NP, meaning all NP problems are solvable in polynomial time. Conversely, if any is not in P, then P does not equal NP. Currently, thousands of real-world problems are NP-complete. No polynomial-time algorithm for any is known, and they are widely believed to be intractable. NP captures a fundamental aspect of computational difficulty: the ease of verifying a claimed solution versus the hardness of finding it. This asymmetry underlies cryptography. Hashing, digital signatures, and proof-of-work all rely on it. One-way functions are believed to exist because verifying a solution is easy but finding it is hard. Practically, NP encompasses many real-world optimization problems such as scheduling, planning, and combinatorial design. These are attacked via heuristics like greedy algorithms, genetic algorithms, and simulated annealing, because exact solutions are believed to be intractable. The P versus NP problem is the Millennium Prize Problem, one of seven offered by the Clay Mathematics Institute. Solving it would resolve fundamental questions about the nature of computation and have immediate applications to cryptography and optimization.
